text: A barge comes in, and for two minutes people keep stepping off it. That is the whole of the film. A.C. Abadie planted a camera where arrivals at Ellis Island had to pass and let the crowd supply the composition — coats, hats, bundles held under the arm, faces turning toward a lens most of them had never met. The camera does not move; it does not need to. The description that travelled with the reel in 1903 called the scene typical and interesting, sales language from men who could not have guessed it would end up in the National Film Registry. Nobody in the frame is performing, because nobody has been told there is anything to perform. Watching is largely a matter of deciding where to look, since the film declines to decide.

A picnic ends in a suicide pact between strangers, and the man survives it. What comes after refuses to settle: drama, then mystery, then romance, then something with the cold of horror in it, with Kim Ki-young treating the borders between them as suggestions. There is an archaeologist, a cave, a skeleton several thousand years old, and a dream in which the dead prove conversational. A hundred and seventeen minutes is a long stretch to keep a viewer unsure which rules are in force, and the uncertainty is the design rather than a symptom of it. The KOFA 100 keeps 살인나비를 쫓는 여자 inside the national record, which is much of the reason it can be found at all. Melodrama is the label the plot wears; almost nothing else about the picture agrees to it.

Nothing happens in these five minutes, and nothing was meant to. John G. Capstaff needed proof that a two-color process — green-blue and red, nothing else — could hold a complexion and a good dress, so the work was done at Paragon Studios in Fort Lee, New Jersey, with women who were already paid to be looked at. Mae Murray, Hope Hampton and Mary Eaton turn, smile and mime at nobody in particular. The reel is an argument addressed to executives. It is also one of the few places where these faces exist in something near their own colouring, which makes it a document of a kind its makers were not aiming for: powder, fabric, the specific red of a 1922 mouth. Demonstration footage catches its subjects at their most arranged and least defended at once.

Ken Jacobs aimed a camera at a projected film from 1905 and kept going for close to two hours. The source was a crowded knockabout chase, the kind of thing staged in one wide setup with everybody in the frame at the same time. Rephotographed, slowed, stopped, pushed until the grain swells into weather, it turns into a place to wander: a hand at the left edge, a figure nobody was meant to notice, the emulsion itself in motion. A hundred and fifteen minutes. Nothing is added and almost everything changes, which is the entire procedure. The catalogue still files it under comedy, and that is not wrong — the old gags are somewhere in there, buried under the attention being paid to them. Attention, at that magnification, is not a neutral act.

A child says her own name until the name comes apart. Gunvor Nelson recorded her daughter Oona reciting the days of the week and the sentence my name is Oona, then cut that sentence into a pulse, a rhythm running under ten minutes of images the way a heartbeat runs under sleep. Repetition does two jobs here at once. It is how a small child takes possession of a word, and it is how a word is emptied out. The film lives in that gap, where delight and fright arrive in the same breath. Ten minutes, no story, a mother filming her daughter and refusing to make her charming. The National Film Registry took it in; the more useful fact is that it is short enough to watch twice in a row, and the second time is not the same film.

Seven films, made across seventeen years, named after nothing but the order in which they were made. Harry Everett Smith began the first in 1939 and finished the last in 1956; each runs between two and six minutes, and they are gathered under a single title as though the gaps between them were part of the work. The numbering goes one to five, then seven, then ten, arithmetic worn on the outside. Twenty-three minutes of shape and colour moving by their own logic. Watched straight through, the set feels less like a programme of shorts than like a man returning to the same question over and over with steadier hands. What changes from one number to the next is easier to notice than to describe, and noticing it is most of the pleasure.

In 1969, four hundred hospital workers in Charleston, nearly all of them Black women and all of them badly paid, walked out over two demands: recognition of their union and a raise. Madeline Anderson filmed it from the inside — she was in the strike, not assigned to it — and the difference shows in how close the camera stands. Thirty minutes. The National Guard arrives, the state government sets itself against the women, and the film keeps returning to the ordinary machinery of holding out, including the support coming from the local Black community. Coretta Scott King, Ralph Abernathy and Andrew Young pass through, and none of them are permitted to take the picture away from the workers whose wages started it. It is a labour film and a civil rights film, and it never has to choose.

Two boys put their faith in a dog they name Promise and enter him in the championship bird dog trials; the dog to beat is the one their own fathers bred and trained. That arrangement is sharper than family pictures usually permit. Georgia Boy is the favourite, and the men's jobs depend on his running as advertised, which sets a child's hope directly against the household income. One field, two dogs, and two outcomes that cannot both arrive. Stuart Heisler takes eighty-one minutes over it and does not soften the arithmetic. The National Board of Review put it among the ten best of 1940, which for a story about kids and a bird dog suggests somebody noticed the second thing running under the first. The dog is the least complicated character in it.

Five minutes, made as coursework, and now held in the National Film Registry. Helen Hill animated it at the California Institute of the Arts, and the ambitions are not modest for a student exercise: animals, the human soul, and a colour sense loud enough to carry both. The humour is light and fast, which is what stops the spiritual business from turning solemn. What a five-minute animated film can do is compress. No exposition, no arc, just a run of images behaving like a blessing said quickly. Student work usually reads as apprenticeship, visible effort aimed at some later and larger film. This one does not read that way at all; it reads as a finished thing that happens to be brief. Nothing about it is waiting to become something else.

The war has been over for years; the writing about it has only started. A Korean veteran of Vietnam is filing a series of newspaper articles about what he did there, converting experience into copy, and the copy calls up a reader: another veteran, who begins appearing in his life without much explanation. Chung Ji-young gives it two hours and lets the two times press against each other, the remembered and the current, so that neither is allowed to be safely finished. The KOFA 100 keeps it in the Korean canon. The real matter is smaller and harder than a war film usually admits: who owns the account of something two men were both inside, and what happens when one of them declines to remain only a reader.

A man comes into Seoul to bring his older brother back to the village and finds the errand was lost before he arrived. The year is 1958, the city is a few years out of a war, and the brother has built something there around a woman who sells herself and a refusal to go home. Shin Sang-ok spends eighty-eight minutes on this without making the countryside innocent or the city damned; what pulls between them is money before it is morality. Two brothers, one woman, and a town short of everything: the geometry gives no sign of holding. The KOFA 100 keeps 지옥화 in the national canon, where it sits as a crime picture largely concerned with what things cost. Nobody in it is choosing freely, and the film is clear about the difference between a choice and a shortage.

Winter on the Hudson, sixteen minutes long. The title is a working term rather than a flourish: this is the first section of a study running across the seasons, and the season chosen to open with is the one that strips the river to water, ice and low light. Peter Hutton lets duration handle what commentary usually handles. Attention drifts, sharpens, then discovers that the surface has changed while it was wandering. Sixteen minutes is short enough to be an exercise and long enough to be a discipline. The river is given the whole frame and the whole running time, which sounds simple and is not. Beginning in winter is a decision: take the version of the river that offers the least and see what the camera can still find. The National Film Registry holds it.
